kurals.tamil:
தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்குத் தான்பிறிது ஊனுண்பான்
எங்ஙனம் ஆளும் அருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannoon perukkarkuth thaanpirithu oonunpaan,
Enganam aalum arul.
kurals.meaning: How can a person who eats the flesh of another creature just to fatten his own flesh ever be ruled by compassion?
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone who says they love animals, but eats one just to grow bigger themselves. That doesn’t fit together, does it? This kural asks exactly that: how can you be truly kind if you make your own body grow by using up another living body?
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a rhetorical question built on a stark bodily symmetry: ஊன் (flesh) appears on both sides of the transaction — தன்னூன் (one’s own flesh) is enlarged by பிறிது ஊன் (another’s flesh). The verb ஆளும் (“rule, govern”) is telling: Valluvar does not ask whether the meat-eater can feel pity occasionally, but whether அருள் (universal compassion, the virtue of the preceding chapter 25) can be the governing principle of his life. Placed in the துறவறவியல் (the section on renunciation), the argument is addressed first to those aspiring to the ascetic ideal, though commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read it as binding on all who claim arul. The logic of feeding self at the cost of other anticipates the Mahabharata’s Anushasana Parva and Ovid’s Pythagoras almost word for word, making this one of the most cross-culturally echoed couplets in the Kural.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That man who seeks to increase his own flesh by (eating) the flesh of others, has to live in this world in great anxiety and after death has to take birth in indifferent races and families.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s discourse on abstaining from meat, the Mahabharata condemns exactly the person who grows his own body by consuming other bodies, and says he pays for it in this life and the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Nearly identical wording to the Kural’s “தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு… பிறிது ஊனுண்பான்” — the same flesh-for-flesh image, with the same moral verdict.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anusasana Parva, Section CXV (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near word-for-word parallel; the Mahabharata stresses karmic consequences where the Kural stresses the contradiction with compassion.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh: For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs warns against people who stuff themselves with meat and wine, saying such self-indulgence ruins a person.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see meat-eating for bodily gratification as morally corrosive, though Proverbs targets gluttony rather than the killing itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match: Proverbs condemns excess, not meat-eating as such; the compassion argument is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Beware of meat. It has addictiveness like the addictiveness of wine.”
islam.explanation: Caliph Umar warned people that meat can become a craving as hard to control as alcohol.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, Umar treats meat as something that enslaves the eater’s appetite, though he counsels moderation rather than abstention.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the concern about appetite for flesh; Islam permits meat, so this is a warning about excess, not a call to renounce it.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells how a calf being led to slaughter hid its head in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s garment and wept; he said, “Go, for this you were created.” Because he showed no compassion, heaven decreed years of suffering on him, which ended only when he later showed mercy to small animals.
judaism.explanation: Even the greatest sage was held accountable for brushing off the fear of an animal about to be killed for food.
judaism.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s claim that one cannot be governed by compassion while treating another creature’s life as simply food for oneself.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on compassion toward animals bound for slaughter; the Talmud does not forbid eating meat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks us to imagine ourselves in the other creature’s place — since all fear death, we should neither kill nor make others kill.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s question presupposes this same act of empathy: the eater’s flesh and the eaten one’s flesh are alike.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Clear ethical overlap on killing; the verse does not mention eating meat directly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Erysichthon cut down Ceres’ sacred oak and was cursed with a hunger that no food could fill; after devouring all his wealth he finally began to tear and eat his own limbs.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows appetite without restraint turning on the eater himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic picture of the Kural’s “feeding one’s own flesh” gone to its end-point: a body fattened by consuming leads to self-destruction.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Thematic only: the myth is about insatiable greed and impiety, not about eating animals.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Oh, how wrong it is for flesh to be made from flesh; for a greedy body to fatten, by swallowing another body; for one creature to live by the death of another creature!”
philosophy.explanation: Ovid puts into Pythagoras’ mouth the core Pythagorean argument for vegetarianism: it is wrong to build one body out of another’s death.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s image — one’s own flesh enlarged by another’s flesh — and the same moral outrage.
philosophy.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (Pythagoras’ teaching; trans. A. S. Kline)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match in both imagery and argument.

kurals.tamil:
பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை அருளாட்சி
ஆங்கில்லை ஊன்தின் பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Porulaatchi potraathaarkku illai arulaatchi,
Aangillai oonthin pavarkku.
kurals.meaning: Just as those who do not guard their wealth cannot enjoy the benefit of owning it, those who eat flesh cannot enjoy the benefit of possessing compassion.
kurals.elementary: If you leave your bicycle out in the rain and never look after it, soon you won’t really have a bike worth riding. In the same way, if you eat animals, you can’t really keep the treasure called kindness — it slips away because you haven’t looked after it.
kurals.university: The couplet works through a precisely balanced parallel: பொருளாட்சி (the enjoyment or sovereignty of wealth) is matched with அருளாட்சி (the sovereignty of grace), and போற்றாதார் (those who do not protect) with ஊன்தின்பவர் (flesh-eaters). The comparison is instructive: wealth is not lost in a single act, but eroded by neglect; likewise compassion is not denied by one meal but hollowed out by a habit that treats life as consumable. The adverb ஆங்கு (“likewise, in that manner”) makes the analogy explicit, a typical Valluvar move from the practical sphere of porul (wealth) to the spiritual sphere of arul. The couplet thus frames compassion as a possession requiring active guarding, a theme found in Buddhist and Mahayana insistence that meat-eating corrodes karuna itself.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The life-breaths of other creatures are as dear to them as those of one's to one's own self.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma reminds Yudhishthira that every creature values its life exactly as we value ours.
hinduism.tie_back: This recognition is what the Kural calls arul; eating flesh means disregarding it, and so losing the possession of compassion.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anusasana Parva, Section CXV (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Supplies the ground of compassion; does not contain the Kural’s wealth analogy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs says a good person cares about the life of his animals, while even the ‘mercy’ of the wicked is really cruelty.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person’s mercy by how they treat animal life — and warns that claimed mercy can be empty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on compassion toward animals; does not address eating them.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that mercy works like a circuit: those who show mercy to what is on earth receive God’s mercy.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat mercy as something one keeps only by practising it; the Kural adds that flesh-eating breaks the practice.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on mercy as a reciprocal possession; Islam does not link it to abstaining from meat.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud (Chullin 84a) derives from the Torah’s wording that a person should not eat meat except when he has a real appetite for it, treating meat as a concession to be used sparingly and not as an everyday entitlement.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching limits casual meat-eating, treating it as something requiring restraint.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s sense that habitual flesh-eating is a moral hazard, though it stops far short of renunciation.
judaism._accuracy_note: Next-best match: restraint rather than abstention; no explicit compassion argument.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “the eating of meat extinguishes the seed of Great Kindness”
buddhism.explanation: In this Mahayana sutra, the Buddha forbids meat to his followers because eating it destroys the root of compassion.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s thesis in Buddhist terms: flesh-eaters cannot keep possession of compassion.
buddhism.source: Mahayana Mahaparinirvana Sutra (as quoted in scholarly summaries; other renderings read “Great Compassion”)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close thematic match; translations vary (“Kindness”/“Compassion”), and Theravada texts take a more permissive view.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But that former age, that we call golden, was happy with the fruit from the trees, and the herbs the earth produced, and did not defile its lips with blood.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek and Roman myth remembered a Golden Age when humans ate only plants and lived in peace with animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The loss of that bloodless age mirrors the Kural’s loss of arul: once flesh is eaten, the gentler state is forfeited.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic, not ethical-analytical; conveys the lost-innocence idea rather than the wealth analogy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Who could wrong a human being when he found himself so gently and humanely disposed toward other non-human creatures?”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that gentleness toward animals trains a gentle character toward people too.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Plutarch treats compassion as one disposition that must be protected in every sphere, including diet.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.7 (996A; Loeb trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on character formation; lacks the wealth parallel.

kurals.tamil:
படைகொண்டார் நெஞ்சம்போல் நன்னூக்காது ஒன்றன்
உடல்சுவை உண்டார் மனம்.
kurals.transliteration:
Padaikondaar nenjampol nannookkaathu ondran,
Udalsuvai undaar manam.
kurals.meaning: Like the heart of one who holds a weapon, the mind of one who has relished the body of another creature does not turn toward goodness.
kurals.elementary: When someone is holding a sword ready to fight, they are not thinking gentle thoughts. The Kural says that someone who enjoys eating another animal’s body is in a similar mood inside — their heart is not turned toward kindness.
kurals.university: Valluvar here moves from action to psychology: the claim is about the state of the மனம் (mind) and நெஞ்சம் (heart). படைகொண்டார் — those who have taken up weapons — is a vivid image of a mind already committed to harm; the flesh-eater who has “tasted the body” (உடல்சுவை) is said to share that orientation. The key word நன்னூக்காது (“does not look toward the good”) implies a turning of attention: pleasure in flesh habituates the mind away from arul. The comparison is striking in a text that elsewhere honours warriors (Porutpaal), showing that Valluvar is describing a disposition, not condemning soldiers; it parallels the Upanishadic idea that food shapes the mind, and the Lankavatara Sutra’s claim that animals fear the meat-eater as they fear a hunter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that when food is pure, the mind (sattva) becomes pure, and from a purified mind comes steady remembrance of the Self (āhāra-śuddhau sattva-śuddhiḥ).
hinduism.explanation: What we eat shapes the quality of our mind.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural similarly claims that relishing flesh shapes the mind, turning it away from goodness like a weapon-bearer’s.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared food-mind link; the Upanishad does not name meat or weapons.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth, and upon every fowl of the air, upon all that moveth upon the earth, and upon all the fishes of the sea; into your hand are they delivered.”
christianity.explanation: When God first permits meat after the Flood, the same passage says that animals will now fear and dread humans.
christianity.tie_back: The Bible links the start of meat-eating to a new relationship of fear — the same weapon-like stance toward other creatures the Kural describes.
christianity._accuracy_note: Interpretive link; Genesis permits meat and does not describe the eater’s mind as corrupted.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah has enjoined goodness to everything; so when you kill, kill in a good way and when you slaughter, slaughter in a good way. So every one of you should sharpen his knife, and let the slaughtered animal die comfortably.”
islam.explanation: Islam permits slaughter but demands ihsan (excellence and kindness) even when the knife is in hand.
islam.tie_back: Both texts worry about the heart of the one holding the blade; Islam answers by disciplining the slaughterer with mercy, the Kural by renouncing flesh altogether.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial overlap: same concern for the knife-holder’s disposition, opposite practical conclusion.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man; he that sacrificeth a lamb, as if he cut off a dog’s neck”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah condemns those who kill animals in ritual while their hearts are far from God, equating it with violence against humans.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Isaiah refuses to separate killing animals from the violent disposition it reveals.
judaism._accuracy_note: Prophetic critique of hypocritical sacrifice rather than of meat-eating per se.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Lankavatara Sutra (chapter 8) argues that the Bodhisattva should not eat meat, because living beings sense the odour of death on the meat-eater and fear him, and because meat-eating is incompatible with the compassion a Bodhisattva must cultivate.
buddhism.explanation: The meat-eater becomes, in the eyes of animals, like a hunter — a figure of threat.
buddhism.tie_back: A striking echo of the Kural’s comparison of the flesh-eater’s mind to that of a weapon-bearer.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close conceptual match; scholars regard this chapter as a later addition to the sutra.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the Athenian Bouphonia (“ox-slaying”) festival, after the sacrificial ox was killed the priest fled, and the axe itself was put on trial and condemned — a ritual acknowledgement of guilt for the killing.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Athenians felt that killing a working ox was close to murder, so they ritually blamed the weapon.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The festival treats the weapon and the killing as morally charged — the same link between blade and heart that the Kural draws.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Ritual guilt over slaughter; the Athenians still ate the ox.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Note that the eating of flesh is not only physically against nature, but it also makes us spiritually coarse and gross by reason of satiety and surfeit.”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that meat-eating dulls and coarsens the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s claim that relishing flesh turns the mind away from goodness.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.6 (995E; Loeb trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the mind-coarsening effect; lacks the weapon image.

kurals.tamil:
அருளல்ல தியாதெனிற் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பொருளல்ல தவ்வூன் தினல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arulalla thiyaathenir kollaamai koral,
Porulalla thavvoon thinal.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what compassion is and what is not: not killing is compassion, killing is its opposite; and eating the flesh of what was killed is not right.
kurals.elementary: What is kindness? Not hurting or killing. What is unkindness? Killing. So eating the meat that came from killing isn’t right either — because it depends on the unkind act.
kurals.university: This couplet has a compressed catechism structure that Parimelazhagar unpacks as: அருள் யாது? கொல்லாமை; அருளல்லது யாது? கோறல் — “What is grace? Non-killing. What is not grace? Killing.” The final clause, பொருளல்லது அவ்வூன் தினல் (“eating that flesh is not porul”), extends the moral judgement from the act of killing to the act of eating, closing the loophole that the eater is innocent because someone else killed. பொருள் here is best read as “righteousness, what is proper” (Varadarasan: அறம் அல்லாதது). The argument prefigures chapter 33 (கொல்லாமை, Non-killing), making flesh-renunciation the dietary corollary of ahimsa.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Meat can never be obtained without injury to living creatures, and injury to sentient beings is detrimental to (the attainment of) heavenly bliss; let him therefore shun (the use of) meat.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu reasons that because meat always requires harming a living being, and harm blocks spiritual reward, one should avoid meat.
hinduism.tie_back: Same syllogism as the Kural: killing is contrary to virtue, meat requires killing, so eating meat is not right.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical logic; Manu elsewhere permits sacrificial meat, which the Kural rejects.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat. And to every beast of the earth… I have given every green herb for meat: and it was so.”
christianity.explanation: In the original creation, God gives humans and animals plants — not each other — as food.
christianity.tie_back: The Edenic ideal of a world without killing for food reflects the Kural’s identification of non-killing with goodness.
christianity._accuracy_note: An ideal of origins; later biblical texts permit meat.

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on [or within] the earth or bird that flies with its wings except [that they are] communities like you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran declares that animals and birds form communities just like human ones.
islam.tie_back: Recognising animals as fellow communities grounds the Kural’s claim that killing them is the opposite of compassion.
islam._accuracy_note: Establishes animals’ moral standing; Islam nevertheless permits lawful slaughter.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Meat was not permitted to Adam, the first man, for consumption”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud reads Genesis 1:29-30 as meaning that the first human was vegetarian; meat was permitted only after the Flood.
judaism.tie_back: Rabbinic tradition thus preserves the ideal that a world without killing for food was the original good — the Kural’s standard.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the ideal; Jewish law later permits meat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “I undertake the precept to refrain from taking life”
buddhism.explanation: The first of the Five Precepts binds every Buddhist not to kill living beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s definition of compassion as non-killing; whether it extends to eating meat is debated within Buddhism.
buddhism.source: Five Precepts (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī), as summarised in scholarship on Buddhist vegetarianism
buddhism._accuracy_note: Exact on non-killing; Theravada does not treat eating unslaughtered-for-you meat as a breach.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For the son of Cronos has ordained this law for men, that fishes and beasts and winged fowls should devour one another, for right is not in them; but to mankind he gave right which proves far the best.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says animals eat each other because they lack justice, while Zeus gave justice to humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod separates the human moral order from the law of devouring — though he applies it to human conduct generally, not to diet.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 276-280 (trans. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: contrasts devouring with justice, but Hesiod did not advocate vegetarianism.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Will ye not cease from this ill-sounding slaughter? See ye not that ye are devouring one another in the thoughtlessness of your hearts?”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles, believing souls pass between humans and animals, calls animal slaughter and eating a form of cannibalism.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he treats killing and eating as one continuous wrong born of a heedless heart.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on killing-and-eating as one wrong; grounded in transmigration rather than compassion alone.

kurals.tamil:
உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை ஊனுண்ண
அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது அளறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Unnaamai ulladhu uyirnilai oonunna,
Annaaththal seyyaathu alaru.
kurals.meaning: The preservation of life rests on not eating flesh; if a person eats flesh, hell, having swallowed him, will not open its jaws to let him out.
kurals.elementary: Many animals stay alive because people choose not to eat them. But the Kural gives a warning too: eating flesh is like falling into a deep, sticky pit that closes its mouth and won’t let you climb back out.
kurals.university: The first line, உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை, is read by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan as “the continued life of beings depends on not eating flesh,” while Karunanidhi reads it socially: because some refrain, many creatures are spared. The second line uses a vivid image: அளறு (literally “mire, bog,” conventionally “hell”) will not perform அண்ணாத்தல் — opening the mouth — to release the one it has swallowed. The mire-image suggests a moral trap from which there is no easy exit, a consequence proportional to the finality of the death inflicted. Comparable ideas of unending or long-lasting punishment for bloodshed appear in Manu’s “mamsah” etymology and in Empedocles’ exile of the blood-polluted daimon.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “'Me he (mam sah)' will devour in the next (world), whose flesh I eat in this (life); the wise declare this (to be) the real meaning of the word 'flesh' (mamsah).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu derives the word for meat (māṃsa) from “me he (will eat)”: the animal you eat now will eat you in the next life.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts warn that eating flesh sets up a consequence that swallows the eater in return.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on retributive consequence; Manu frames it as reversal of roles, the Kural as a hell that does not release.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence.”
christianity.explanation: In the parable of the rich man, who “fared sumptuously every day” and ignored suffering at his gate, the rich man ends in torment and cannot cross back.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s image of a place of punishment that does not let its captive go, earned by self-indulgence without mercy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Next-best: parallel on irreversible punishment; the parable concerns neglect of the poor, not meat.

islam.quote_or_event: “A lady was punished because of a cat which she had imprisoned till it died. She entered the (Hell) Fire because of it”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that cruelty to a single animal can lead a person into Hell.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the death of an animal at human hands to a hellish consequence for the human.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on hell for cruelty to animals; not about eating meat.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And while the flesh was yet between their teeth, ere it was chewed, the wrath of the LORD was kindled against the people, and the LORD smote the people with a very great plague.”
judaism.explanation: When the Israelites in the wilderness demanded meat, they were struck down while still eating the quail; the place was named Kibroth-hattaavah, “graves of craving.”
judaism.tie_back: The craving for flesh leads directly to a pit of death — close to the Kural’s image of the swallowing mire.
judaism._accuracy_note: The sin is ingratitude and craving, not meat-eating as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One who, while himself seeking happiness, oppresses with violence other beings who also desire happiness, will not attain happiness hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says harming others for one’s own happiness blocks happiness in future lives.
buddhism.tie_back: Parallels the Kural’s warning that the flesh-eater’s future is closed off.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Karmic consequence of violence; not explicitly about meat, and not an eternal hell.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus’ crew, starving, slaughtered and ate the sacred cattle of the Sun; as punishment they all died and never returned home.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic picture of the Kural’s warning: eating forbidden flesh brings a doom from which there is no return.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The offence is sacrilege against a god’s herd, not meat-eating generally.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “whenever one of the daemons, whose portion is length of days, has sinfully polluted his hands with blood… he must wander thrice ten thousand seasons from the abodes of the blessed”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles taught that a soul stained by bloodshed is exiled through countless lifetimes before it can return to bliss.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts describe a long captivity for those who shed blood; the Kural’s mire “will not open its mouth.”
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on prolonged punishment for bloodshed; Empedocles speaks of exile and rebirth, not a single hell.

kurals.tamil:
தினற்பொருட்டால் கொல்லாது உலகெனின் யாரும்
விலைப்பொருட்டால் ஊன்றருவா ரில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thinarporuttaal kollaathu ulagenin yaarum,
Vilaipporuttaal oondraruvaar il.
kurals.meaning: If the world did not kill for the sake of eating, no one would kill and supply flesh for the sake of money.
kurals.elementary: Why does a shop sell something? Because people buy it. If nobody bought meat, nobody would kill animals to sell it. So the person who buys is part of the reason the animal was killed.
kurals.university: This is the most analytical couplet of the chapter, and it answers a specific excuse: “I did not kill; I only bought meat already killed.” Valluvar identifies the causal chain — தினற்பொருட்டு (for the sake of eating) generates விலைப்பொருட்டு (for the sake of price) — so that the consumer’s demand is the root cause of the butcher’s act. G. U. Pope’s translation makes the rebuttal explicit (“Who’d kill and sell, I pray, if none came there the flesh to buy?”). The argument is strikingly modern, anticipating demand-side ethics, and directly contests the Theravada allowance of meat not seen, heard or suspected to be killed for oneself; it closely matches Manu 5.51, which counts the buyer among the slayers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who permits (the slaughter of an animal), he who cuts it up, he who kills it, he who buys or sells (meat), he who cooks it, he who serves it up, and he who eats it, (must all be considered as) the slayers (of the animal).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu spreads the guilt of the killing across the whole chain, including buyer, seller and eater.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s point: buying and eating make one a participant in the slaughter.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on shared responsibility across the supply chain.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says it is better to give up meat if eating it harms others.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Paul holds the eater responsible for the wider effects of his eating — though his concern is fellow believers, not animals.
christianity._accuracy_note: Honest note: Paul elsewhere (1 Cor 10:25) allows eating whatever is sold in the market without question, which runs against the Kural’s argument.

islam.quote_or_event: “There is no person who kills a small bird or anything larger, for no just reason, but Allah will ask him about it.”
islam.explanation: Every killing of an animal must have a legitimate purpose, and each will be accounted for before God.
islam.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s insistence that the purpose behind killing matters morally; Islam accepts eating as a just purpose, the Kural does not.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial: accountability for killing, but food is explicitly a “just reason” in this hadith.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When the LORD thy God shall enlarge thy border… and thou shalt say, I will eat flesh, because thy soul longeth to eat flesh; thou mayest eat flesh, whatsoever thy soul lusteth after.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah frames ordinary meat-eating as a permission granted to human craving, which many rabbinic and later thinkers (e.g., Rav Kook) read as a concession rather than an ideal.
judaism.tie_back: The text itself locates the origin of killing in the eater’s desire — the same causal root the Kural identifies.
judaism._accuracy_note: Grants permission rather than forbidding; the ‘desire drives killing’ reading is interpretive.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a lay follower should not engage in five types of business. Which five? Business in weapons, business in human beings, business in meat, business in intoxicants, and business in poison.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha forbids lay followers from trading in meat as a livelihood.
buddhism.tie_back: Targets the same “killing for price” the Kural names; but the Jivaka Sutta permits monks to eat meat not killed specifically for them, which the Kural’s demand argument implicitly rejects.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on the seller’s side; Theravada does not extend the ban to buyers.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus divided a slaughtered ox so that humans kept the meat and the gods received only bones wrapped in fat; from then on sacrifice fed human appetite while appearing to honour the gods.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth explains why sacrificial meat ends up on human tables.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It exposes how human appetite drives the killing behind a respectable pretext — as the Kural exposes the buyer’s excuse.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Next-best: aetiological myth about meat and sacrifice; no ethical condemnation of demand.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “What a terrible thing it is to look on when the tables of the rich are spread… And it is even more terrible to look on when they are taken away, for more is left than has been eaten. So the beasts died for nothing!”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch points out that the killing is driven by the appetite and display of diners, who waste much of what was slaughtered.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, he places responsibility for the slaughter on the consumers whose demand causes it.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.4 (994F; Loeb trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on consumer responsibility; lacks the explicit market logic of buyer and seller.

kurals.tamil:
உண்ணாமை வேண்டும் புலாஅல் பிறிதொன்றன்
புண்ணது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Unnaamai vendum pulaaal pirithondran,
Punnathu unarvaarp perin.
kurals.meaning: If people truly understood that flesh is nothing but the wound of another creature, they would refrain from eating it.
kurals.elementary: If you saw a hurt animal with a sore, you would never want to eat that sore. The Kural says meat is really just that — a wound cut from another living creature. If we remembered that, we wouldn’t want to eat it.
kurals.university: The force of the couplet lies in a single noun, புண் (wound, sore, ulcer). By renaming meat as “another creature’s wound,” Valluvar strips away the culinary vocabulary that disguises its origin, a technique of moral re-description. The conditional உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (“if one gains those who perceive / if one comes to perceive”) makes the argument depend on clear perception: the problem is not ignorance of a rule but a failure to see what is in front of us. The metrical lengthening in புலாஅல் (alapedai) lingers on the word “flesh,” as if forcing the reader to look at it. Plutarch and Ovid’s Pythagoras make the very same move, calling meat “sores” and “pitiful wounds.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Having well considered the (disgusting) origin of flesh and the (cruelty of) fettering and slaying corporeal beings, let him entirely abstain from eating flesh.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu tells the reader to reflect on where meat comes from — the binding and killing of living beings — and then to give it up entirely.
hinduism.tie_back: Same method as the Kural: once one sees the true origin of flesh, the desire to eat it should end.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close in method; lacks the specific ‘wound’ image.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.”
christianity.explanation: Daniel and his friends refuse the Babylonian king’s meat and wine and ask for vegetables and water instead, and emerge healthier.
christianity.tie_back: An example of deliberate refusal of meat as a matter of conscience, though Daniel’s concern is ritual purity rather than the animal’s wound.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel in act, not in reason.

islam.quote_or_event: “Prohibited to you are dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, and [those animals] killed by strangling or by a violent blow or by a head-long fall or by the goring of horns…”
islam.explanation: The Quran forbids blood, carrion and animals killed violently, focusing attention on how an animal died.
islam.tie_back: Both texts ask the eater to look at the death and bleeding behind the meat; Islam responds with purity laws, the Kural with abstention.
islam._accuracy_note: Next-best: shared attention to blood and wounding; Islam permits properly slaughtered meat.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat.”
judaism.explanation: Even when meat is permitted, the Torah forbids eating it with its blood, because the blood is the animal’s life.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists that meat is bound up with another creature’s life and must not be eaten as if it were mere food.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the life-in-the-flesh insight; draws a restriction rather than abstention.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Taking life, beating, wounding, binding, stealing, lying, deceiving, worthless knowledge, adultery; this is stench. Not the eating of meat.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Amagandha Sutta, a Buddha answers a vegetarian Brahmin by saying true impurity lies in evil deeds, not in eating meat.
buddhism.tie_back: An honest counterpoint: this early text denies that meat itself defiles, whereas the Kural insists meat is inherently a wound — yet it still lists wounding and taking life as the real impurity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Counterpoint rather than parallel; included for honesty about intra-Buddhist diversity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Pythagoras compares flesh-eaters to the Cyclops Polyphemus, who devoured Odysseus’ companions raw: people “tear, with cruel teeth, at pitiful wounds, recalling Cyclops’s practice.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The monstrous cannibal Cyclops becomes a mirror for ordinary meat-eating.
greek_mythology.tie_back: By invoking the Cyclops, the myth makes the eater see the torn body in front of him — the Kural’s ‘wound.’
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline); Homer, Odyssey 9
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Mythic comparison drawn by a philosopher-character; the Cyclops story itself is about cannibalism.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “How was it that the pollution did not turn away his taste, which made contact with the sores of others and sucked juices and serums from mortal wounds?”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch asks how the first meat-eater could bear to put the sores and wounds of another creature to his lips.
philosophy.tie_back: Precisely the Kural’s image: flesh is another creature’s wound, and seeing it so should end the appetite.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.1 (993B; Loeb trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the ‘wound’ image and the argument from perception.

kurals.tamil:
செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார் உண்ணார்
உயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த ஊன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyirin thalaippirindha kaatchiyaar unnaar,
Uyirin thalaippirindha oon.
kurals.meaning: Those whose vision has been freed from delusion and fault will not eat flesh that has been separated from life.
kurals.elementary: When your eyes are clear, you see things as they really are. People whose minds are clear and free from wrong ideas look at meat and see a body that was once alive — so they don’t eat it.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on an elegant repetition: தலைப்பிரிந்த (“separated from”) occurs in both lines — the wise are separated from செயிர் (fault, delusion), while the flesh is separated from உயிர் (life). The parallel suggests a moral symmetry: purity of vision is achieved by the same act of separation that, done to a living being, produces flesh. காட்சியார் (“those of vision”) links the virtue to perception, continuing kural 257’s theme that seeing clearly ends the desire for meat. Parimelazhagar glosses செயிர் as the delusion (mayakkam) that makes one mistake the body for the self, placing this couplet within the ascetic epistemology of the துறவறவியல்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is beyond duality and doubt, whose mind is engaged within, who is always busy working for the welfare of all sentient beings, and who is free from all sins, achieves liberation in the Supreme.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita describes sages whose impurities are destroyed (kṣīṇa-kalmaṣāḥ) and who delight in the welfare of all beings (sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ).
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s “those freed from fault” are the same figures, and their concern for all beings excludes eating them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the purified sage; the Gita verse does not mention diet.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But let all except the very weak and the sick abstain altogether from eating the flesh of four-footed animals.”
christianity.explanation: St Benedict’s monastic rule forbids monks the meat of four-footed animals, a practice kept for centuries in Western monasticism.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, those who commit to purity of life and vision renounce flesh.
christianity._accuracy_note: Ascetic discipline rather than compassion for animals; fowl and fish were often allowed.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram.”
islam.explanation: Pilgrims in the consecrated state of ihram are forbidden to hunt or kill game.
islam.tie_back: Islam links a heightened state of purity with refraining from killing animals — a limited echo of the Kural’s pure-sighted who refuse flesh.
islam._accuracy_note: Temporary ritual restriction on hunting, not a permanent renunciation of meat.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s teaching that an ignoramus is prohibited from eating meat, deriving from Leviticus 11:46 (“This is the torah of the beast and of the fowl”) that only one who engages in Torah study may eat animals and fowl.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic tradition ties the permission to eat meat to spiritual knowledge and discipline.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts connect meat and wisdom — but in opposite directions: the Talmud limits meat to the learned; the Kural says the truly wise abstain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Next-best; an inverted parallel, included for its link between knowledge and meat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is not noble who injures living beings. He is called noble because he is harmless towards all living beings.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the noble one (ariya) by harmlessness toward all beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, spiritual excellence is defined by refusing to harm living creatures.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on harmlessness as the mark of the noble; diet not specified.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod’s golden race of mortals lived “like gods,” free from toil and grief, while the fruitful earth gave them its harvest unforced; later Pythagorean writers took this age as a model of bloodless living.
greek_mythology.explanation: The first, purest human race lived on what the earth freely gave.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The purest humans of myth, like the Kural’s fault-free sages, live without killing for food.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Hesiod does not explicitly say the golden race abstained from meat; the vegetarian reading comes from later writers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Can you really ask what reason Pythagoras had for abstaining from flesh? For my part I rather wonder both by what accident and in what state of soul or mind the first man who did so, touched his mouth to gore”
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch reverses the burden of proof: it is not the abstainer but the meat-eater whose state of mind needs explaining.
philosophy.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s assumption that a clear, undeluded mind naturally refuses flesh.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, On the Eating of Flesh I.1 (993A-B; Loeb trans.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close on the link between mind and abstention; Plutarch argues from nature and pity rather than liberation.

kurals.tamil:
அவிசொரிந் தாயிரம் வேட்டலின் ஒன்றன்
உயிர்செகுத் துண்ணாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Avisorindh thaayiram vettalin ondran,
Uyirsekuth thunnaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Not to kill a single creature and eat it is better than performing a thousand sacrifices with offerings poured into the fire.
kurals.elementary: Some people think doing big, fancy religious ceremonies makes them very good. The Kural says: sparing just one animal’s life, and not eating it, is better than a thousand of those ceremonies.
kurals.university: This couplet makes a pointed comparison with Vedic ritual: அவி (havis, oblations such as ghee) poured into the fire in a thousand வேள்வி (yajñas, sacrifices). By ranking the simple restraint of not killing one creature above a thousand sacrifices, Valluvar subordinates ritual merit to ethical conduct — a critique shared with the Jain and Buddhist movements and with the later Upanishadic interiorisation of sacrifice. The numerical contrast (ஆயிரம் versus ஒன்றன் — “a thousand” versus “one”) is characteristic of Valluvar’s rhetoric of disproportion. Manu 5.53 offers a strikingly similar valuation, equating lifelong abstention from meat with a century of horse-sacrifices, while the Hebrew prophets and Jesus prefer “mercy, and not sacrifice.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who during a hundred years annually offers a horse-sacrifice, and he who entirely abstains from meat, obtain the same reward for their meritorious (conduct).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu equates lifelong abstinence from meat with a hundred years of the grandest Vedic sacrifice.
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same comparison as the Kural: abstention from flesh outweighs vast ritual offerings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Manu says ‘equal’ where the Kural says ‘better’.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice”
christianity.explanation: Jesus quotes Hosea to say God values mercy over ritual offerings.
christianity.tie_back: Same ranking as the Kural: compassion outweighs sacrifice.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on mercy over ritual; not specifically about animals or diet.

islam.quote_or_event: “Their meat will not reach Allah, nor will their blood, but what reaches Him is piety from you.”
islam.explanation: The Quran says God receives none of the sacrificial animal’s meat or blood — only the worshipper’s inner devotion.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares that the outward offering is worthless compared with the inner moral state.
islam._accuracy_note: Relativises sacrifice but still commands it; does not advocate abstention.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”
judaism.explanation: Hosea says God prefers loving-kindness (ḥesed) to animal offerings.
judaism.tie_back: The same prophetic ranking of compassion above ritual that the Kural expresses.
judaism._accuracy_note: Ethical priority matches; Hosea does not call for abstaining from meat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kutadanta Sutta, the Buddha tells a Brahmin of a great ancient sacrifice in which no oxen, goats, fowl or pigs were slain and no trees cut; only ghee, oil, butter, curds and honey were offered — and then teaches that giving, virtue and the precepts are still greater sacrifices.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines sacrifice as bloodless and ultimately ethical.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks not killing above ritual offerings.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong parallel in critique of animal sacrifice; not specifically about eating meat.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “It is not enough to have committed such wickedness: they involve the gods in crime, and believe that the gods above delight in the slaughter of suffering oxen!”
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Pythagoras attacks animal sacrifice as dragging the gods into human cruelty.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s rejection of the idea that killing for ritual can be meritorious.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV (trans. A. S. Kline)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close on critique of sacrifice; lacks the explicit ‘better than a thousand’ comparison.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the altar did not reek with pure bull's blood, but this was held in the greatest abomination among men, to eat the goodly limbs after tearing out the life.”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles describes a golden age when worship was bloodless and killing to eat was the worst abomination.
philosophy.tie_back: Joins sacrifice and meat-eating in one condemnation, as the Kural does.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close: bloodless worship and killing-to-eat as abomination.

kurals.tamil:
கொல்லான் புலாலை மறுத்தானைக் கைகூப்பி
எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kollaan pulaalai maruththaanaik kaikooppi,
Ellaa uyirum thozhum.
kurals.meaning: All living beings will fold their hands and worship the one who neither kills nor eats flesh.
kurals.elementary: Imagine every animal in the world putting its paws together to say “thank you” to one person. That’s the picture here: the person who never kills and never eats animals is loved and honoured by every living thing.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with an image of cosmic reverence: எல்லா உயிரும் (all living beings) perform கைகூப்பித் தொழுதல் — the joined-palm gesture of worship. The two qualifications, கொல்லான் (one who does not kill) and புலாலை மறுத்தான் (one who has refused flesh), sum up the chapter and anticipate the next section on கொல்லாமை. The hyperbole of animals folding hands is deliberate: the one who renounces power over other lives receives from them the honour usually given to gods. Parallel visions appear in Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, Empedocles’ age when “all things were tame and gentle to man,” and the Buddhist teaching that one who cultivates goodwill is dear to human and non-human beings alike.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He for whom no one is put into difficulty … is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says the person who causes no living being distress is especially beloved of God.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the one who harms no creature receives the highest honour.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Honour comes from God rather than from all creatures; diet not mentioned.

christianity.quote_or_event: In the Little Flowers of St Francis, birds gather around Francis as he preaches to them, stretching their necks and bowing their heads, and do not fly away until he blesses them; later tradition tells of the wolf of Gubbio made gentle by him.
christianity.explanation: Christian legend pictures creatures responding with reverence to a saint of radical gentleness.
christianity.tie_back: A near-literal image of the Kural’s “all living beings worship him.”
christianity.source: The Little Flowers of St Francis (Fioretti), ch. 16 and ch. 21
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong image match; Francis was not a strict vegetarian, and the stories are hagiographic.

islam.quote_or_event: “Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate (living being).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet told of a man forgiven by God for giving water to a thirsty dog, and taught that kindness to any living creature is rewarded.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see kindness to all living beings as earning the highest esteem; in Islam the honour comes from God.
islam._accuracy_note: Parallel on reward for kindness to animals; not about abstaining from meat or creatures’ reverence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid… They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea.”
judaism.explanation: Isaiah envisions a messianic age when no creature harms another.
judaism.tie_back: The peaceable kingdom is the social form of the Kural’s ideal: a world where no one kills, honoured by all creatures.
judaism._accuracy_note: A cosmic vision rather than a statement about an individual renunciant.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings. The devas protect one.”
buddhism.explanation: Among the eleven benefits of cultivating goodwill (metta), the Buddha lists being beloved by humans and non-humans and protected by the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural’s promise that the non-harming person is revered by all living beings.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on universal affection; the cause is goodwill in general, not specifically abstaining from meat.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orpheus, the legendary singer linked to the Orphic way of life that abstained from killing, drew wild beasts, birds, trees and stones to gather around him in peace when he sang.
greek_mythology.explanation: Myth pictures all nature gathering in rapt attention around the gentle Orpheus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of all creatures honouring one figure of harmlessness, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The creatures are drawn by music, not by his non-violence; the Orphic abstention link is from later tradition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For all things were tame and gentle to man, both beasts and birds, and friendly feelings were kindled everywhere.”
philosophy.explanation: Empedocles recalls an age of Love when humans did not kill, and in return every creature was friendly toward them.
philosophy.tie_back: The same reciprocal harmony the Kural promises: renounce killing, and all creatures become your friends.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Describes a golden age rather than an individual; close in spirit.
